reference.source: Kelley & Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology / vasculitis guidance
clinicalPearls: Wheals persist beyond 24 hours, unlike ordinary urticaria which resolves within hours
Lesions often burn or feel painful rather than simply itch and may leave bruising or pigmentation as they fade
Skin biopsy shows leucocytoclastic vasculitis of small dermal vessels
Most cases have normal complement levels and a relatively benign, skin-limited course
Systemic features such as arthralgia, angio-oedema, or abdominal pain can accompany the rash
Underlying triggers include connective tissue disease, infection, drugs, and rarely malignancy
Distinguishing it from chronic spontaneous urticaria changes both investigation and management
reference.pathophysiology: Urticarial vasculitis is an immune complex-mediated small-vessel vasculitis affecting the postcapillary venules of the dermis. Deposition of immune complexes activates complement and recruits neutrophils, producing leucocytoclastic inflammation with vessel wall damage, fibrin deposition, and extravasation of red cells that accounts for the residual bruising. The persistent inflammatory infiltrate explains why the wheals last longer than in ordinary urticaria. The normocomplementaemic form is usually skin-limited, whereas complement consumption signals a greater likelihood of systemic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous small-vessel (leucocytoclastic) vasculitis of other cause
Autoinflammatory syndromes such as Schnitzler syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy for histology and direct immunofluorescence
Complement levels (C3, C4, CH50) and C1q assessment
Antinuclear antibody and connective tissue disease serology
Full blood count, inflammatory markers, and renal function with urinalysis
Hepatitis serology and other infection screening when indicated
Serum and urine electrophoresis if a paraproteinaemic association is suspected
redFlags: Low complement suggesting the hypocomplementaemic systemic subtype
Renal involvement with proteinuria or haematuria
Pulmonary symptoms or breathlessness suggesting systemic disease
Systemic features pointing to underlying lupus or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Normocomplementaemic, skin-limited urticarial vasculitis usually follows a self-limiting or relapsing but benign course. Cases with low complement or systemic involvement carry greater morbidity and require closer monitoring and more intensive therapy.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for ordinary urticaria and treating with antihistamines alone
Failing to biopsy atypical or persistent wheals
Not checking complement, thereby missing the hypocomplementaemic systemic subtype
Overlooking an underlying connective tissue disease, infection, or drug trigger
references: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference vasculitis nomenclature
management: Identify and treat any underlying cause, such as connective tissue disease, infection, a culprit drug, paraproteinaemia or malignancy
Use antihistamines for symptomatic relief, recognising they are often insufficient alone
Treat mild, skin-limited, normocomplementaemic disease with NSAIDs, colchicine, dapsone or hydroxychloroquine

Treat systemic or hypocomplementaemic disease with corticosteroids and a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant such as azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil or methotrexate, escalating to rituximab or other biologics for refractory cases
Monitor complement levels, renal function and urinalysis to detect systemic and renal involvement
Refer to rheumatology for confirmed systemic or hypocomplementaemic disease
